title: 71% of surveyed emerging-market firms use AI. How deeply are they adopting it?
gist: IFC's survey of 1,666 PE/VC-backed emerging-market firms finds 71% use AI (up from almost 40% a year earlier), but adoption is shallow: only 10% of internal adopters have embedded it across core processes. Skills, not cost or infrastructure, are the top barrier.

insights.claim: In IFC's latest survey of 1,666 PE/VC-backed emerging-market firms, 71 percent report using AI, up from almost 40 percent in the survey a year earlier.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: AI diffusion among EM venture/PE-backed firms is moving from niche to mainstream within a year.

insights.claim: Half of all AI adopters among surveyed emerging-market frontier firms say they began using AI during 2025, indicating a very recent adoption wave.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Most adopters are new, so deployment maturity lags headline adoption rates.

insights.claim: Frontier firms are typically first to adapt global technologies to local contexts and pave the way for other firms to follow, making them a leading indicator of broader EM diffusion.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Track PE/VC-backed EM firms as an early signal for wider AI uptake in developing economies.

insights.claim: 57 percent of internal AI adopters and 45 percent of external adopters are still experimenting or deploying AI only on a limited scale.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Headline adoption overstates real transformation; productivity payoffs are still ahead for most firms.

insights.claim: Only 10 percent of internal adopters have embedded AI across core internal processes, and 19 percent of external adopters describe AI as core to their business model.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: The deep-adopter cohort is small, so it is the segment to watch for outsized gains.

insights.claim: The authors frame adoption as a ladder and ask whether frontier firms and the firms around them will climb or stall on its lower rungs.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Use rung-of-the-ladder depth, not binary usage, to assess AI exposure of EM companies.
insights.quote: Together, these efforts will help determine whether frontier firms, and the wider population of firms around them, climb the AI ladder or stall on its lower rungs.

insights.claim: Skills shortages are the most frequently cited barrier to AI adoption, ahead of costs or technical infrastructure; more than four in ten non-adopters name them as their main obstacle versus about one quarter of adopters.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Human capital, not capex or compute access, gates EM AI adoption, favouring training and talent plays.
insights.locator: What prevents firms from moving further

insights.claim: Around 70 percent of surveyed firms report staff regularly use AI applications, about half can integrate AI into business processes, and only 30 percent can build AI solutions in-house.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Capability falls sharply at each step up the ladder; in-house builders are a scarce minority.
insights.locator: The skills needed for AI adoption

insights.claim: Without continued skills development, today's adoption gap could become a deeper divide between firms that simply use AI and those that leverage it to innovate and improve business outcomes.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Expect divergence in outcomes among EM firms, concentrating gains in those with in-house capability.

insights.claim: Firms using AI more extensively are more likely to say their current adoption level is appropriate, which may reflect selection of more capable firms, experience, or in shallow adopters limited awareness of what deeper use could offer.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Self-reported barrier answers are unreliable guides to unmet demand for AI tooling.

insights.claim: 43 percent of AI adopters deliberately upskill existing employees, while only 9 percent rely mainly on hiring specialists and 1 percent on outsourcing.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Training providers beat recruiters and outsourcers as the main channel for EM AI capability building.
insights.locator: The survey shows that many firms

insights.claim: About half of adopting firms lack a deliberate AI capability strategy: 24 percent expect employees to do more within existing roles and 23 percent make no significant workforce changes.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Many adopters are under-investing in organizational change, limiting realized returns.

insights.claim: It is unclear whether upskilling alone can build the capabilities needed to adapt AI to a firm's operations; hiring AI specialists and strengthening managerial skills may be needed to reach an AI-native model.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Look for demand for senior technical and managerial talent as the next bottleneck.

insights.claim: 93 percent of AI adopters self-report positive business outcomes, with productivity improvement the most cited benefit (54 percent) far ahead of product innovation (15 percent).
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Gains so far are efficiency-led; self-reported figures may be upward-biased.

insights.claim: Deeper AI adopters are more likely to report innovation benefits, and product innovation, more than efficiency gains alone, is how AI is likely to drive firm growth.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Growth upside accrues to deep adopters, not broad shallow usage.

insights.claim: Investors can help portfolio companies by sharing expertise, identifying use cases and supporting access to talent, while policymakers should strengthen human capital and innovation ecosystems.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: PE/VC value-add on AI capability is a differentiator for EM portfolio performance.
